label: Psychology
title: Why Capable People Feel Like Frauds – The Impostor Phenomenon
description: Why do so many capable people feel that they do not really deserve their success – and that one day they will be found out? In this calm video essay we look at the 1978 paper by Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes that first described the impostor phenomenon, why it is not a clinical diagnosis, how common it seems to be, its close link to perfectionism, and why Socrates offers a healthier way of not knowing.

sections.text:
You get the job. You pass the exam. Someone praises your work in front of the whole team. And instead of pride, a quiet thought arrives: they have made a mistake. Sooner or later, someone will notice that I do not really belong here.

If you have ever felt this, you are in large company. Many of the people you admire most have felt it too.

Psychologists have studied this feeling for almost fifty years. And the most interesting part is not how common it is. It is what it gets wrong about knowledge, and about ourselves.

sections.heading: Two Psychologists and a Pattern
sections.text:
In 1978, the psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes published a paper with a striking title: The Imposter Phenomenon in High Achieving Women.

Over several years, they had worked with more than 150 women who were successful by any outside measure. They had degrees, awards, respected positions. And yet many of them were convinced that they were not truly intelligent. They believed they had fooled everyone around them.

When something went well, they explained it away. It was luck. It was timing. Someone had overestimated them. When something went badly, it was proof of what they had suspected all along.

Clance and Imes gave this pattern a name: the impostor phenomenon. Their paper focused on women, because those were the people they had worked with. But later research made clear that the experience is not limited to women. Men report it too, as do students, doctors, artists and researchers.

What made the pattern so puzzling was the gap between the outside and the inside. From the outside, these were people others turned to for answers. From the inside, every achievement felt like a narrow escape, and every new challenge felt like the moment the mask would finally slip.

sections.heading: Not a Diagnosis
sections.text:
Today, most people call it impostor syndrome. But the word syndrome is a little misleading.

The impostor phenomenon is not a mental disorder. It does not appear in the diagnostic manuals that clinicians use. It describes an experience, a way of interpreting your own success, that many people go through at certain points in their lives.

That matters. A feeling that comes and goes, often when we start something new, is very different from an illness. Calling it a phenomenon reminds us that it is something we notice and can examine, not a fixed label we carry.

How common is it? Honestly, nobody knows the exact number. In 2020, a team led by Dena Bravata reviewed 62 studies on the topic. Depending on the questionnaire and the cutoff used, the reported rates ranged from 9 to 82 percent. That huge range tells us two things. The feeling is widespread. And it is hard to measure precisely.

sections.heading: The Perfectionism Trap
sections.text:
One of the most consistent findings in this research is a link to perfectionism.

People who hold themselves to extremely high standards are more likely to report feeling like an impostor. And it is easy to see why. If the standard is flawless, then every result falls short. Every success contains some small error, and that error becomes the real story.

Clance later described a kind of cycle. A new task arrives. Anxiety follows. Some people overprepare, working far more than necessary. Others put things off until the last moment and then rush. Either way, the task goes well.

But the success does not count. The overpreparer thinks: it only worked because I worked so hard. The procrastinator thinks: it only worked because I got lucky. Neither learns the simple lesson that might be true: I was capable.

And so the next task brings the same fear, and the cycle begins again.

sections.heading: A Wiser Kind of Not Knowing

quote.lead: Around 2,400 years ago, Socrates told the court in Athens how the oracle at Delphi had called him the wisest of men. He was puzzled, so he questioned people with a reputation for wisdom. His conclusion is famous.
quote.text: I seem, then, in just this little thing to be wiser than this man at any rate, that what I do not know I do not think I know either.
quote.author: Plato, Apology 21d

sections.text:
At first glance, this might sound like impostor thinking. Socrates, too, says he does not know very much.

But look closer, and the two are almost opposites.

The impostor feeling is not really humility. It is a hidden certainty. It says: I know that I am not good enough, and I know that others are wrong about me. It claims a knowledge of ourselves that we do not actually have.

Socratic humility is different. It is simply honest. It says: here is what I know, here is what I do not know yet, and that is all right. There is no shame in the gap. The gap is where learning begins.

The impostor hides what they do not know, and fears being exposed. Socrates spent his life saying it out loud, in public, and turning it into a question.

There is also a practical difference. The person who fears exposure tends to avoid questions, because a question might reveal a gap. The person who accepts the gap asks freely, and so learns faster.

sections.heading: Small Ways to Loosen Its Grip
sections.text:
So what can you do when the feeling returns? These are not cures, just a few ways of looking at it more clearly.

First, notice the timing. The impostor feeling often appears at thresholds: a new job, a promotion, a first project. In those moments, feeling unsure is not a sign that you do not belong. It is a sign that you are learning something new.

Second, keep a plain record. Write down what you actually did, and what actually happened. Not how it felt, just the facts. Over time, this gives you evidence that is harder to explain away as luck.

Third, say it to someone. The feeling thrives in silence. Often the person you tell will answer: me too. And suddenly the secret loses much of its weight.

And finally, borrow the Socratic sentence. Instead of, I am a fraud, try: there are things here I do not know yet. It is more accurate. And it is a lot kinder.

None of this makes the feeling vanish overnight. But each time you name it, it becomes a little more like weather passing through, and a little less like a verdict about who you are.

sections.heading: Allowed to Be Learning
sections.text:
Perhaps the deepest mistake of the impostor feeling is the idea that real experts never doubt. That somewhere there are people who feel completely sure, and that you are the only one pretending.

But most people are figuring things out as they go. The surgeon on her hundredth operation, the writer on his fifth book, the teacher in front of a new class: each of them meets moments they have never quite met before. The ones who seem most confident often have simply made peace with not knowing everything.

You do not have to be finished to belong where you are. You are allowed to be learning. That is not a sign that you are an impostor. It is what every honest mind looks like from the inside.

short.title: Why capable people feel like frauds
short.hook: Feel like you'll be found out?
short.text:
In 1978, two psychologists described a strange pattern. Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes worked with highly successful women who were convinced they had fooled everyone around them.

They called it the impostor phenomenon. It is not a mental disorder. It is an experience, and men and women both report it.

It is often linked to perfectionism. If the standard is flawless, every success feels like luck.

Socrates offered a healthier way of not knowing: what I do not know, I do not think I know either.

You do not have to be finished to belong. You are allowed to be learning.
